title: What is “green steel”?
summary: “Green steel” is steel produced with significantly lower carbon emissions than the way most steel is made today. The end-product is the same as steel made in conventional ways – what changes is how the steel is made.
body_markdown:
## Why is lowering steelmaking emissions a challenge?


About 70% of the world’s steel is still made using the coal-intensive BF-BOF route. These processes are proven, reliable, deeply embedded in global supply chains, and the most efficient way of making steel today – so they're challenging to displace.


At the same time, the world still needs steel – it’s essential for urbanisation, infrastructure development and the transition to low-carbon energy systems needed to support growing populations.


To meet this demand with low-emissions steel at scale, there are some practical hurdles to overcome:


### 1. The technology is still maturing


The most promising new pathways – including hydrogen-based direct reduction, electric smelting furnaces and electrolysis – are in pilot or early commercial stages.


### 2. It requires huge amounts of low-carbon energy


Steelmaking is highly energy-intensive, and decarbonising it depends on the availability of competitively-priced renewable electricity, natural gas or hydrogen. Not every region has the energy mix or infrastructure in place yet.


### 3. It’s more expensive – for now


Low-emissions steel currently costs more to produce than conventional steel because it relies on newer technologies, large volumes of renewable electricity, and new infrastructure like hydrogen production and storage. The International Energy Agency estimates these cleaner methods can currently cost around 50–140% more than coal-based steelmaking, depending on the technology and location. However, as technology matures and carbon penalties rise, the new lower-emission technology could become more cost competitive.


### 4. It’s a whole value-chain challenge


Steelmaking depends on a network of industries, including mining, energy, transport and manufacturing. Cutting emissions isn’t as simple as one company switching to renewables, or changing one step in the process. It requires major collaboration between all parties involved to make changes across the whole value chain, alongside significant time, investment and infrastructure.
